title: Consumer Finance Survey Report 2021
tldr: A comprehensive nationwide survey of the financial condition of Filipino households, covering income, expenditure, assets, liabilities, and financial attitudes during the COVID-19 pandemic.
problem_and_motivation: There was a lack of comprehensive data on household wealth and indebtedness in the Philippines. The existing FIES and APIS surveys had limited coverage on assets and liabilities. The survey aimed to address these data gaps and inform evidence-based socio-economic policies.
approach: The survey used a two-stage cluster sampling design with 18,000 households drawn from the 2013 Master Sample Frame by the PSA.
Data were collected via face-to-face Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) from March to December 2022.
The primary unit of analysis was the Primary Economic Unit (PEU), comprising financially interdependent household members.
Survey instruments were translated into six major Philippine languages and included 255 items across demographics, income, expenditure, assets, liabilities, and financial attitudes.
Data validation used a two-stage approach: first-stage consistency checks and second-stage focus group discussions for qualitative insights.
Weighted estimates with coefficients of variation of 20 percent or below were considered precise per PSA standards.
findings: Average household income was P189,842 per year (P15,820 per month), with a median of P144,000.
Average household expenditure was P230,905 per year (P19,242 per month), with food at home accounting for 55.4% of total spending.
Wage employment was the leading income source for 91.5% of households, up from 73.7% in 2018.
Only 29.3% of households carried any form of debt, a substantial decrease from 40.4% in 2018.
Deposit account ownership rose to 35.3% in 2022 from 9.7% in 2018, while e-money account ownership grew to 24.3% from 0.3%.
The Gini coefficient was estimated at 0.422, indicating significant income inequality.
Average household size was 4.1, lower than 4.5 in the 2018 CFS.
Homeownership rate was 69.9%, with 85.8% of homeowners fully owning their residence.
The average net worth of Filipino families was P435,346 with a median of P120,200.
Only 2.0% of households had emergency savings equivalent to at least three months of living expenses.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This report provides the most comprehensive quantitative portrait of Filipino household finances, covering income, expenditure, assets, liabilities, and financial attitudes using a nationally representative sample of 18,000 households. It tracks changes in household financial condition between 2018 and 2021, capturing the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. The report offers statistically reliable estimates at national and sub-national levels, including for the first time all regions of the Philippines. It also presents methodological contributions such as income inequality analysis using multiple measures (Gini, Theil, interdecile ratios) and equivalence scale comparisons for expenditure.
directly_justifies: 55.4% of household spending went to food at home, the largest expenditure category.
Only 29.3% of households carried debt, down from 40.4% in 2018.
E-money account ownership grew from 0.3% to 24.3% between 2018 and 2022.
Gini coefficient of 0.422 indicates significant income inequality in the Philippines.
Only 2.0% of households had emergency savings for three months of expenses.
limits: Data collected during pandemic may not reflect typical household financial conditions.
Self-reported data may be affected by recall bias and intentional under/over-reporting.
Limited coverage of financial investments data, estimates have high coefficients of variation.
Does not provide individual-level or algorithm-specific data for ML model training.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. Flagged as high relevance: 1.A (Filipino Young Professionals as a Demographic) due to detailed age, sex, education, and health data; 1.B (Financial Structure) due to comprehensive income, expenditure, asset, and liability data; 1.C (Financial Behavior) due to coverage of financial attitudes, risk preferences, and savings/investment behavior. Flagged as medium relevance: 2.A (Culturally Specific Financial Practices) for references to paluwanga, sangla-ATM, and sari-sari stores; 2.D (Filipino Spending Cycles) for expenditure breakdown on celebrations, gifts, and special occasions; 3.A (Expense Categorization Frameworks) for the PCOICOP classification and essential/non-essential distinction. Considered and rejected: All algorithm-related topics (4.A-6.B, 8.A-9.C, 14.A-14.C) because the paper is a survey report with no algorithmic contribution; 7.A-7.E (Budget Recommendation) because while budgeting data exists, no computational budget recommendation is proposed; 10.A-10.C (Data Privacy) only mentioned in passing regarding BSP advisory; 11.A-13.C (Engagement, Evaluation, Savings Goals) not directly addressed. The report's main contribution is to Philippine household finance data, not to any algorithmic or computational method.

limitations: Data collection occurred during COVID-19 pandemic restrictions, potentially skewing results [unacknowledged].
Self-reported values may be affected by recall bias and intentional misreporting.
Estimates with CVs greater than 20% are flagged as imprecise.
The survey does not provide individual-level behavioral data for personal finance system development [unacknowledged].
Lack of longitudinal panel data limits causal analysis of financial behavior changes [unacknowledged].
